THE RULE: every terminal ends in questions for an attorney, never a conclusion; no node grades a plan; banned phrases: 'you should/need', 'we recommend', 'in your case', 'your plan is missing'. hrefs are relative to /ny/prepare/. maxDepth asserted at load.

t_incapacity_agents_sp.title: Naming your decision-makers — and their backups
t_incapacity_agents_sp.mechanism: As a single parent, no spouse steps in by default if you can't make your own medical or financial decisions. Those decisions fall to the people you name: a health care agent under a health care proxy (New York names one agent at a time, with successors behind them), and a financial agent under a durable power of attorney, which can name a successor. Both operate only while you are alive and end at death. If the first-named person can't serve and no backup is named, authority can fall to no one until a court appoints someone.

explainers.label: Why a power of attorney and a health care proxy both end at death
See the incapacity states on the timeline

attorneyQuestions: Who is my first health care agent and my first financial agent, and who is the named backup behind each if that person can't serve?
Given that New York doesn't allow co-agents on a health care proxy, how should I order my choices?
worthConfirming: Worth confirming: whether my power of attorney is durable, so it keeps working precisely when I can't act.
Worth confirming: whether each document names at least one backup, so authority doesn't rest on a single person being available.

t_guardianship_sp.title: For a single parent, the incapacity gap has no fallback
t_guardianship_sp.mechanism: A guardian named in a will operates at death. If you are alive but temporarily unable to care for your children, the will hasn't spoken — and as a single parent there's no second parent to step in. New York fills that gap with a separate instrument: a standby guardian designation under SCPA 1726, which can be written to operate on incapacity rather than at death, and runs alongside your own rights so it can end when you recover. Without one, no one holds clean legal authority over your children until a court acts.

explainers.label: Why a will's guardian doesn't operate during incapacity
See the incapacity state on the timeline

attorneyQuestions: Does my plan cover who cares for my children if I'm alive but incapacitated, not only if I die?
Would a standby guardian designation under SCPA 1726 fit my situation, and who should it name?
worthConfirming: Worth confirming: whether the guardian named in my will and any standby designation name the same people, in the same order.
Worth confirming: whether any standby designation is written to end when I recover.

t_other_parent.title: A surviving parent's rights and your guardian nomination are two different things
t_other_parent.mechanism: When your children's other parent is living and has parental rights, that changes the picture. A guardian named in a will is a nomination — courts weigh it heavily — but a surviving legal parent generally has priority for custody over a non-parent named in a will. How your nomination and the other parent's rights interact turns on facts a general tool can't weigh, which is exactly what a first meeting with an attorney is for.

explainers.label: Why a will's guardian doesn't operate during incapacity

attorneyQuestions: Given that my children's other parent is living, how does my guardian nomination interact with their parental rights?
Are there steps that would make my wishes clearer or more likely to be followed, and what are their limits?
worthConfirming: Worth confirming: who currently holds legal custody and parental rights, and whether any court order already addresses it.
Worth confirming: whether my reasons for my nomination are written down somewhere an attorney can review.

t_childrens_money_sp.title: Who raises your children and who manages their money can be two separate roles
t_childrens_money_sp.mechanism: In New York, a guardian raises the children but does not automatically control the money left for them. A trustee manages and disburses those funds under the trust's terms — often a 'health, education, maintenance, and support' standard. As a single parent you're choosing both roles from scratch, and they are often, deliberately, different people. When and how children receive money outright is set by the trust, and the common patterns — staggered ages, a protective lifetime trust, or a single 'pot' held until the youngest reaches a set age — trade autonomy against protection rather than being right or wrong.

explainers.label: See the both-parents-gone state on the timeline

attorneyQuestions: Should the person who raises my children and the person who manages their inheritance be the same person or two different people?
Which distribution pattern fits my family — staggered ages, a protective lifetime trust, or a common pot held until the youngest reaches a set age?
worthConfirming: Worth confirming: whether the plan names a trustee, and a backup trustee, separately from the guardian.
Worth confirming: whether the ages or terms for distributions are written into the trust rather than left to be decided later.

x_business.title: This is where a walkthrough should hand off to your attorney
x_business.body: A business or professional practice adds questions this tool doesn't cover — succession, a buy-sell agreement, valuation, and how the interest passes without disrupting the business. That is exactly what a first meeting with an attorney is for, so it's worth walking in with it named rather than working around it here.
attorneyQuestions: How should my business interest pass at death or incapacity, and is a buy-sell or succession agreement in place?
Does owning the business change who should serve as my agent, executor, or trustee?

x_out_of_state.title: This is a question for your attorney, not this tool
x_out_of_state.body: Real property in a second state can require a separate probate under that state's law, and this walkthrough is built for New York only. That's precisely the kind of thing a first meeting should spend its time on, so it's worth naming up front.
attorneyQuestions: Does my out-of-state property expose my estate to a second (ancillary) probate, and can a trust avoid it?
Which state's law governs that property, and does it change who inherits it?

x_special_needs.title: This deserves specialized attention, not a general walkthrough
x_special_needs.body: When a child or beneficiary has a disability or special needs, an ordinary inheritance can unintentionally affect eligibility for means-tested benefits. Planning for this uses specialized tools and belongs with an attorney experienced in it — which is a reason to seek that person out, not a shortcoming in your planning.
attorneyQuestions: Would a supplemental or special-needs trust protect this beneficiary's eligibility for benefits while still providing for them?
How should gifts from relatives be directed so they don't unintentionally disrupt those benefits?

x_taxable.title: Once estate tax is in play, this is attorney territory
x_taxable.body: New York has its own estate tax, separate from the federal one and with a 'cliff' — above a threshold, the exclusion can phase out entirely. The current figures live on the Sources page. When an estate may cross that line, the planning becomes tax planning, which is exactly what an attorney (often with an accountant) is for.

explainers.label: Current estate-tax figures and when they were last verified

attorneyQuestions: Is my estate likely to owe New York estate tax, and does the cliff apply to me?
Are there planning steps — trusts, gifting, how assets are titled — that change the exposure?
